idiom_name: pRetry(fn, {retries, factor, minTimeout, randomize, maxRetryTime, signal})
implementation_notes: The idiom is a higher-order wrapper around an async function: pRetry(fn, options) re-invokes fn (which receives the attempt number) until it resolves or the budget is spent, with exponential backoff controlled by factor, minTimeout, maxTimeout and randomize, a maxRetryTime wall-clock budget measured on a monotonic clock, and AbortSignal support so a cancelled caller stops the loop. Classification is expressed by throwing AbortError (stop, do not retry) or through the shouldRetry and shouldConsumeRetry predicates, while onFailedAttempt exposes attemptNumber, retriesLeft, retriesConsumed and retryDelay for logging; makeRetriable(fn, options) attaches the same policy permanently to a function. Defaults matter in practice - retries is 10 and minTimeout 1000ms - so the library is already opinionated out of the box, and a caller that wants three quick attempts must say so. The classic hand-rolled loop is replaced by the wrapper; write it by hand only when the retry must interleave with other control flow.
pitfalls: The defaults (retries: 10, minTimeout: 1000, factor 2) make a naive pRetry(fn) wait many minutes in the worst case: set retries and maxRetryTime deliberately.
Non-network TypeErrors abort retries by design, but other permanent errors are only aborted if you throw AbortError or return false from shouldRetry - an unclassified 404 is retried ten times.
The wrapped function receives the attempt number but no cancellation token: pass an AbortSignal into fetch and into the options, or the loop keeps running after the caller gave up.
unref is off by default, so pending retry timers keep a Node process alive; set unref: true in short-lived scripts and CLIs.

variants.name: undici RetryAgent dispatcher policy for Node fetch
variants.idiom_name: new RetryAgent(new Agent(), {maxRetries, minTimeout, timeoutFactor, retryAfter, methods})
variants.implementation_notes: Node's built-in fetch is backed by undici, so the policy can live in the dispatcher instead of the call: RetryAgent wraps another dispatcher and installs a RetryHandler per request, re-dispatching failures that match the policy - maxRetries (default 5), minTimeout (500ms) with timeoutFactor (2) for the growing delay, retryAfter (true) to honour the Retry-After header, a methods allow-list that already excludes POST and PATCH, retryable statusCodes (500, 502, 503, 504, 429) and transport errorCodes (ECONNRESET, ECONNREFUSED and friends). The caller's code does not change - it still calls fetch - and the retry decision is declared once for every request through that agent, which is the form to prefer when the whole process talks to the same flaky dependency; the trade-off is that classification is limited to status and error codes, with the retry callback as the escape hatch.
pitfalls: A RetryHandler instance is designed for a single request and must not be reused across requests; RetryAgent constructs one per dispatch for that reason.
throwOnError defaults to true, so the final failed attempt throws instead of returning the response - code that wants to inspect a 503 body must disable it or supply a custom handler.
The default statusCodes list omits 408 and the default methods list excludes POST/PATCH/CONNECT: widening either is a deliberate decision, and widening methods accepts duplicate side effects.
Retries happen below fetch, so an application-level AbortSignal still applies to the whole sequence and can cut a retry short in the middle of its delay.
